planting.note: Direct sow outdoors around the last frost date since this fine-rooted annual resents transplanting, and make successive sowings every few weeks for a continuous supply of cut flowers.

directions: Scatter seed directly where plants are to grow in light, well-drained, slightly alkaline soil, since the fine taproot rarely survives being moved. Unlike the familiar perennial baby's breath of florist bouquets, this fast annual species flowers within weeks of sowing, sending up slender branching stems topped in a haze of tiny single white or pale pink blooms. Thin seedlings to a few inches apart and stake lightly in exposed sites, as the airy stems can flop in wind and rain. Cut regularly for arrangements or let a few plants go to seed, as it self-sows readily in a loose cottage-garden bed.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring in moist, fertile soil and give it room, since established clumps form tall, self-supporting stands that take a couple of seasons to reach full height.

directions: Set out in rich, evenly moist soil in full sun to light shade, where it will slowly build into an upright clump of whorled foliage topped by branching candelabra spikes. 'Fascination' bears pale lilac-pink flowers that give the tiered flower spikes a softer, warmer tone than the white-flowered species, making it a favorite among designers building naturalistic perennial borders. The stiff stems rarely need staking, and the plant is long-lived once settled, so choose a permanent spot rather than one requiring frequent division. Leave the seed heads standing through winter for structure and for seed-eating birds.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in consistently moist, humus-rich soil and stake in windy sites, since this is one of the taller Culver's root selections and can lean once in full bloom.

directions: Grow in rich, moisture-retentive soil in full sun, where its whorled leaves and narrow lavender-blue flower spikes rise well above most border perennials. 'Lavendelturm', German for 'lavender tower', was selected for its soft blue-violet bloom color and height, and reads as a vertical accent among rounder-flowered companions like phlox and echinacea. It establishes slowly from a crown but, once settled, persists for many years without needing to be lifted. Deadheading is unnecessary; the dried flower spikes add winter interest and the plant is virtually untroubled by pests or disease.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in moist, humus-rich soil in a site with some afternoon shade, since leopard's bane foliage can scorch in hot, dry summer sun.

directions: Plant in cool, moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun where summers aren't too hot, since this old garden cultivar is one of the earliest daisy-flowered perennials to bloom, often opening before many spring bulbs have finished. 'Miss Mason' produces unusually large, bright golden-yellow blooms on sturdy stems above heart-shaped basal leaves, and is more vigorous and floriferous than typical seed-grown Doronicum. The clump tends to go dormant and disappear in hot midsummer, especially in warmer zones, so mark its location and avoid disturbing the roots. Divide every few years in fall to keep the planting vigorous and to share the long-lived cultivar with other gardeners.

planting.note: Plant small divisions or rooted cuttings in spring into lean, gritty, very well-drained soil, since soggy winter conditions are far more likely to kill it than cold.

directions: Site in poor, sharply drained soil in full sun, the same conditions that keep its felted, silvery-white, scallop-edged leaves tight and compact rather than lush and floppy. This low, spreading relative of culinary horehound is grown almost entirely for its soft, woolly foliage rather than its small, inconspicuous summer flowers, making it a useful filler along the edge of a rock garden, gravel path, or sunny wall. It is remarkably drought tolerant once rooted in and resents rich soil or overhead irrigation, which encourages rot and loose, leggy growth. Shear lightly after flowering to keep the mat dense and encourage fresh silver foliage.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun, where the tidy clump holds its shape without staking or division for several years.

directions: Grow in average to lean, well-drained soil in full sun, where this compact species forms a neat clump of narrow, grass-like leaves topped from midsummer on by bright yellow, daisy-like flowers on short stems. It is much better behaved in a border than its taller, coarser cousin elecampane (Inula helenium), staying low and dense rather than spreading aggressively. Established plants tolerate short dry spells but bloom more heavily with regular moisture, and the flowers are attractive to bees and small butterflies. Little care is needed beyond an occasional spring tidy-up of old foliage; division is rarely necessary and mainly done to propagate new plants.
